GINKGO

The tree that outlived the dinosaurs — a field guide from the Ginkgo Grove at Blandy Experimental Farm
Looking straight up into the gold — a mature ginkgo at Blandy Experimental Farm, November 4, 2026. Photo taken in the grove.
🎧 Listen — the ceiling of gold (0:24)

Start Here: A Ginkgo Journey

On November 4, 2026, at the peak of the fall color, we walked the Ginkgo Grove at Blandy Experimental Farm — the State Arboretum of Virginia — with a camera and a list of questions. Why were twenty trees dead on one side of the grove? Why were baby bald cypresses planted in cages among them? What did the little metal tag nailed to a trunk mean? This guide is everything those questions uncovered: a complete education in the ginkgo tree, built from the evidence of that walk. Ginkgo is the subject. Blandy is the classroom.

🎧 The Comprehensive Teaching — “Ginkgo: The Tree That Outlived the Dinosaurs”

One long audio lesson — about thirty minutes — tying the whole guide together: deep time, the two trees of Charlottesville, the fifty-year experiment, the strange sex life of a living fossil, the dying side of the grove, and what this tree means to people. Press play and let it teach.

Shorter companions from the same day: the grove-walk answer and the tree-tags addendum are woven into the sections below, and every photograph carries its own short teaching clip.

The view from under the gold: fan leaves against a November sky at peak color. Ginkgoes turn as one tree and drop as one grove — after the first hard frost, a stand like this can shed nearly every leaf in a single night. Tap to enlarge.

Meet the Ginkgo

🌿Botanical nameGinkgo biloba L.
🧬Family / OrderGinkgoaceae — the only living species in the order Ginkgoales
🏯Also calledMaidenhair tree · silver apricot (China) · temple tree
🗺️Native toChina — a few mountain refuges; cultivated across East Asia for 1,000+ years
🌲Kind of treeDeciduous gymnosperm — a naked-seed tree, kin to conifers, not a flowering tree
⚥SexesDioecious — each tree is male or female; sex hidden for ~20 years from seed
📏Size66–115 ft tall (20–35 m); great age brings massive, spreading crowns
⏳Lifespan1,000+ years; temple trees in China are documented far beyond that
🌎HardinessUSDA zones 3–8 · full sun · the toughest street tree in the temperate world
🍂Fall colorClear luminous yellow — and the whole tree can drop in a single night after hard frost
🚨ConservationListed Endangered in the wild (IUCN) — while planted by the million in cities

The leaf is the signature: a fan split into two lobes — biloba — with veins that radiate from the stalk and fork again and again but never join into a network. That dichotomous venation is a plumbing design from before flowers existed. Leaves on the stubby spur shoots are usually entire; leaves on the long, reaching shoots carry the deep cleft. Goethe, who wrote the tree's most famous poem in 1815, saw in that one-leaf-in-two a symbol of unity inside duality.

The ginkgo leaf, drawn to the tree's own plan: two-lobed fan, forking veins, entire spur leaf, and the female's golden seeds.
The same leaf, alive: rain beading on a fan in close-up. Look for the notch and the veins that fork but never join. Photo: Wikimedia Commons (CC0).
🎧 Listen — reading a leaf (0:30)
🈚 Where the name comes from. In Japanese the tree is ginkyō — “silver apricot,” for the pale, apricot-like seeds. Kaempfer wrote the name down in the 1690s, and in his handwriting, scholars believe, the y was read as a g — so the West has called it Ginkgo ever since: a world-famous name born from a copyist's slip, carried home from Japan by the man in the People section below.

Ginkgo Timeline

🎧 Listen — 270 million years in one look (0:38)
~270 M yrs ago
Ginkgo's order, the Ginkgoales, appears in the fossil record — before dinosaurs, mammals, or flowers.
Jurassic
Ginkgo-like trees grow worldwide — Europe, Asia, North America, Australia. Dinosaurs walk under them.
By 7 M yrs ago
Cooling climate and rising flowering plants squeeze the family out — gone from North America, then Europe by ~2 million years ago.
China, centuries
One species survives in mountain valleys — and in temple gardens, where monks plant and tend it for a thousand years. Gardeners carry a species through the bottleneck.
1690s
Engelbert Kaempfer, a German physician in Japan, gives the West its first description of the tree — and its name.
~1730
A ginkgo grows at Utrecht in the Netherlands — Europe's first. Kew plants one in the 1760s that still lives.
1784
America's first ginkgo is planted at the Woodlands estate in Philadelphia.
1815
Goethe presses a ginkgo leaf into a letter with his poem “Gingo biloba” — the leaf becomes a European emblem of love and unity.
~1860
William A. Pratt plants the Pratt Ginkgo by the Rotunda at the University of Virginia — the University's first memorial tree.
1896
Sakugoro Hirase discovers the ginkgo's sperm swims — a fern-like trait no other tree on the continent kept.
1929
Orland E. White plants the seed of a UVA female at Blandy — the experiment that becomes this grove.
1945
A ginkgo less than a mile from the Hiroshima hypocenter, blasted and burned, buds again the next spring. Its seeds now travel the world as peace ambassadors.
1980s
Blandy's final tally: 157 females, 144 males — the answer White waited a lifetime for, delivered after his death.
2026
The grove still stands at Blandy — thinning on its wet side, replanted with bald cypress, still being read. This guide is written under its canopy.

Roots in Asia — where the tree was kept alive

  • ⛩️Temple trees. When the wild species faded to a few Chinese mountain refuges, monks planted ginkgoes at temples across China, Japan, and Korea — and gardened a species through the bottleneck.
  • 🥢A food and a medicine. The inner nut — ginnan in Japan, baiguo in China — is eaten in modest amounts at celebrations, and the leaf entered Asian herbal practice centuries before it entered Western supplements.
  • 📜A tree of scholars. Planted at academies and shrines, the ginkgo became East Asia's emblem of endurance, peace, and a long life of learning.
  • 🌱Still wild, barely. China's Tianmu Mountain trees may be the last truly wild stand — which is why a seed-grown grove in Virginia matters to the species' future.
The ancestor in stone: Ginkgo adiantoides, a fossil ginkgo leaf. The fan shape in this rock is the same fan on Blandy's trees. Photo: Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA).

Two Trees of Charlottesville

Every origin story in this grove hangs on one distinction — and it is the correction this guide is proudest to print.

On the northwest corner of the Rotunda stands the Pratt Ginkgo: planted about 1860 by William A. Pratt, the University's first Superintendent of Buildings and Grounds, honored as the University's first memorial tree, and still turning the most brilliant yellow on the Lawn each fall. It is also, in the University's own words, “a male tree, so it does not produce those round fruits.” The Pratt has never borne a seed in its life.

So the Blandy grove did not descend from the Pratt. The records say the seed came from a female ginkgo on the University of Virginia's Grounds — a mother whose name, if she had one, nobody preserved. The most famous ginkgo in Virginia is a childless monument; the valley of gold at Blandy is the family of an unnamed mother. There is one honest postscript, labeled as possibility and nothing more: the Pratt was a mature male shedding pollen over those same Grounds in the years that mother set her seed — so the monument may be the grove's unrecorded father. Unprovable. Unrecorded. Biologically wide open.

~1860
Pratt Ginkgo planted by the Rotunda
1 mother
an unnamed UVA female — the grove's only recorded parent
300+
of her children standing at Blandy today

White’s Experiment

In 1929, plant geneticist Orland E. White, Blandy's first director, asked a question with a catch: if you plant one female ginkgo's seeds, what share of her children are male, and what share female? He predicted one to one. The catch: a ginkgo hides its sex for twenty years or more, so the answer required planting an orchard and outwaiting a career.

Planting waveTreesNote
192940First seedlings from the UVA mother
1933220The great planting
1935156
1938–39108Completes the original 524
1947114Replacements for early losses
Total638Each one tagged and mapped

White directed Blandy until 1955 and died without his answer. The scientific census (Santamour and colleagues, 1983) counted 359 alive in 1982 — 56% survival — and when the survivors were finally sexed in the 1980s: 157 females, 144 males. One to one, as predicted — delivered half a century late, by the tags.

Inside the grove — rows planted in waves between 1929 and 1947, photographed November 4, 2026.

Family Tree

Every tree in the grove shares one mother. That single fact makes Blandy's grove a family — and it decides what happens when you take its seeds home.

What the tree means, genetically

  • 🧬All 638 are at least half-siblings. Every one took half its inheritance from the same UVA mother; the other half came from whichever Charlottesville male's pollen was on the wind — so no two Blandy trees are alike, yet all are family.
  • 🌰Take a grove seed home and you plant a grandchild. A seed from a Blandy female is half that female — and she is herself half the mother — so your sapling carries about a quarter of the original mother's inheritance. On the tree above, it belongs one full row below the grove: Generation 2.
  • ♂The fathers are the wild card. The Pratt Ginkgo — UVA's great male by the Rotunda — was shedding pollen on those Grounds in exactly those years. He may be a father of this grove: possible, unprovable, and honestly labeled.
  • ⚠️Closeness cuts both ways. If a grove male fathers seed on a grove female, the parents are half-siblings and the child is closer still. That is why arboreta track pedigrees — and why those trunk tags matter far beyond names.
  • 🏯One mother is also the point. White's design — one known mother, many fathers — turned a grove into a controlled experiment. Every seed collected here extends a family whose paperwork reaches back to a single tree in Charlottesville.

Sex and Seeds

Ginkgo reproduction is machinery the other seed plants abandoned. In spring the males shed pollen from dangling clusters; on the females, pairs of ovules wait on slender stalks. Inside the ovule, the tree does something astonishing, discovered in 1896: its sperm swims — two large cells, crowned with thousands of beating hairs, swim through a droplet to reach the egg. Only ginkgoes and cycads still reproduce this way, a method inherited from the ferns.

The fertilized ovule ripens into what looks like a small golden plum. It is not a fruit — ginkgoes are gymnosperms and never evolved one — but a seed in a fleshy coat rich in butyric acid, the compound behind the famous rancid-butter smell. Inside the coat sits the silver-white nut, a food in Asia for centuries, eaten in modest amounts. We found these seeds ourselves, scattered in the leaf litter under the grove's female half — the next generation, lying in the gold.

How these seeds germinate

1. Collect ripe seeds in fall, after they drop. 2. Clean the fleshy coat away (wear gloves — the coat can irritate skin, and it is the source of the smell); the hard inner nut is the true seed. 3. Give it winter: cold, moist stratification — about 60–90 days in damp medium in the refrigerator — mimics the season the seed evolved to wait through. 4. Sow shallow in well-drained mix, keep moist, and wait for spring warmth. 5. Be patient twice over: seedlings grow slowly, and their sex stays secret for roughly twenty years — White's whole experiment in one seed packet. A grafted, named male cultivar is the shortcut for anyone who wants a guaranteed fruit-free tree.

Where Ginkgo Thrives

Ginkgo is famous for tolerating almost anything — drought, road salt, air pollution, compacted city soil. It has exactly one non-negotiable demand: drainage. Learn that one rule and you can read this entire grove like a report card.

SunFull sun — 6+ hours; young trees accept light shade
SoilDeep and well-drained above all; adapts to loam, sand, or clay once drainage is right
pHBroadly tolerant — mildly acidic to mildly alkaline (about 5.5–7.5)
WaterModerate and consistent while young; drought-tolerant once established; never standing water
RootsDeep-rooting; dislikes transplanting once large — plant young, plant once
ToleratesHeat, salt spray, pollution, poor urban air — nearly pest-free
Fails inWet, poorly drained ground — roots suffocate and decline crown-first

Compatible company — plant by moisture, not by looks

  • ☀️On the same drained ground: the arboretum's other sun-lovers — oaks, lindens, and the great conifer collection nearby.
  • 💧At the wet margin: the water guild — bald cypress first of all, with dawn redwood and river birch — trees that take the moisture ginkgo refuses.
  • 🍂Under the canopy: the grove chooses its own ground layer — turf, and its golden leaf-fall returning as mulch each November.

The rule for any planting, garden or arboretum: match the tree to the water in the soil, not the picture in the catalog.

The grove's edge — planted rows meeting brush and wild understory, with neighboring collections beyond. Blandy, November 4, 2026.

The Grove's Neighbors

The grove does not grow alone — it keeps company with some of the arboretum's oldest residents and its newest arrivals. Did they grow up together? Mostly, yes: this is a designed landscape, planted in collections from 1927 on, maturing side by side — not a wild forest that happened.

  • 🌲Cedar of Lebanon allée — the elders on the walk in. Thirty-six cedars line the path to the grove, planted as the young arboretum took shape. They and the ginkgoes are contemporaries — two collections of the same founding era, grown old in sight of each other.
  • 🌊Bald cypress — the newcomers. The rust-orange row behind the dead stand, and the caged sapling in our photograph, are this decade's plantings: a southern swamp native moved in because the ground is wet. Documented by the grove's own strategy — and by our camera.
  • 🦕Dawn redwood — the other living fossil. Known from fossils before it was found alive in China in the 1940s, so every dawn redwood here is younger than the grove's first plantings — a fossil's grandchild generation, catching up fast.
  • 🌳Oaks, lindens, and the great conifer collection — the dry-ground guild. On the grove's higher side, the arboretum's sun-loving collections share the drained soil ginkgo demands. Neighbors are chosen by water, not by looks — the Thrives section's zoning again.
The newcomer in its fall dress: a bald cypress gone rust-orange. It reads as an evergreen all summer, then drops its needles like any deciduous tree — the right tree for the grove's wet ground. Tap to enlarge.
An elder's name plate: Cedar of Lebanon, Cedrus libani, on one of the allée trees. The cedars and the ginkgoes are founding-era contemporaries — and Blandy labels them the same way, at chest height, in metal. Tap to enlarge.
🔍 What we saw vs. what the records say. Documented: the collections were planted from 1927 under White; the grove's census (638 planted, 359 alive in 1982) is published; the cypress replacement is visible and verifiable on the ground today. Inference, labeled: the exact planting year of individual neighbor rows is not in the public sources we could check — the allée's age is read from the arboretum's history and the trees' own size. When a Blandy planting ledger surfaces, this section gets dates.

Grove Lifecycle

The evidence in one frame: green holdouts at left, a dead ginkgo snag at center, a caged bald cypress sapling in the foreground, the established rust-orange cypress row behind — and the gold grove beyond. November 4, 2026.
🎧 Listen — the dying side (0:27)

Our walk began with this photograph and one question: why are roughly twenty trees dead on one side of the stand? The records give the frame: the grove has been thinning since youth — 638 planted by 1947, only 359 alive by the 1982 census — and the published study honestly recorded that the causes of death could not be determined from the records.

  • 📸The pattern: roughly twenty dead trees, clustered on one side of the stand — not scattered through it.
  • 🪵The corpses: grey snags, dead from the crown down — the signature of roots failing, not of trunks breaking.
  • 🗓️The ages: the plantings spanned 1929–1947 — mixed ages do not die together by age.
  • 🦠The species: ginkgo is famously pest-free — no disease we know signs its name in a cluster like this.

The best-supported explanation — labeled inference: it is the water. Trees planted across a decade, of mixed ages, do not die in a cluster by age, and a nearly pest-free species does not die in a cluster by disease. What clusters is soil. This old field's low side holds water too long and too often; ginkgo, for all its toughness, declines in wet ground crown-first — exactly the top-down death written on that grey snag. The bald cypress is the land's own answer: a deciduous conifer of southern swamps that wants the water, turns rust-orange in fall, and is already thriving in a row behind the dead stand.

The grove on paper — why one side died

One drawing teaches the whole section. The grove is one field with two kinds of ground — and the dead trees are not scattered. They are clustered, exactly where the ground stays wet:

🟡 healthy ginkgo✕ dead ginkgo🔺 new bald cypress💧 seasonal ponding
A teaching diagram drawn from our November 4 walk and the drainage rule — labeled inference, not a survey. The rescue follows the map: cypress takes the wet ground (bottom right), ginkgo keeps the dry.

The replacement strategy, as the grove itself is executing it

Five steps, run as a wheel — each one feeds the next, and the wheel never stops. Tap a word in the wheel to jump to its step.

READ — the evidence first. Census the losses tree by tree against the tag records before changing anything. The grove's own numbers set the scale: 638 planted by 1947, only 359 alive by the 1982 census — a collection that counts itself honestly can heal itself honestly.

ZONE — by moisture, not by habit. Map the wet ground and say out loud what it is. What clusters is soil — the low side of this old field holds water too long, and replanting ginkgo into the same wet pocket would only repeat the failure.

MATCH — right tree, right place. Bald cypress takes the wettest gaps, because cypress wants the water; ginkgo replants go only on drained ground. The goal is not to restore the map of 1939 — it is a grove slowly becoming two groves, gold and rust, each in the ground it was made for.

GUARD — protect the young. Every new sapling wears a wire cage against deer rub, exactly like the caged cypress in the foreground of the photograph above. A replacement tree is a promise; the cage is how the grove keeps it.

RECORD — everything, always. Each replacement gets its tag and its file, so the next generation inherits the evidence, not just the outcome. Then the wheel turns again: next year's census is next year's READ.

The Tag on the Trunk

Stop at almost any tree at Blandy and you will find a small metal tag nailed to the trunk. It looks like nothing — and it is the most important thing on the tree. The tag is the tree's name, its library card, and its medical chart, all pressed into one strip of metal. Here is the one we photographed, turned flat so you can read it:

Tag ID #9558 — photographed hanging on its ginkgo, then turned sideways so the stamped numbers read left to right. Tap the photo to see it full-size.
🏷️ Meet tag #9558. The number is this tree's individual ID — one tree, one number, never reused. The tree wearing it is a ginkgo in Blandy's western grove (the gold canopy on this guide's cover is its crown). Behind the number sits the tree's file in Blandy's plant records: species, where its seed came from, when it was planted, where it stands on the map, its sex, its measurements, its health. The public window into those records is the arboretum's online Tree Finder, where the collection is mapped tree by tree; the full ledger itself is kept by Blandy's Plant Records Officer. Think of the tag as a library card: the card is on the tree, but the book — the tree's whole biography — is in the office.
🎧 Listen — the tag (0:21)

How the tags are made

Blandy says it in one sentence: “All trees are labelled with an embossed tag. Each tag has two numbers — one refers to the group and year that the plant came in, the other is its individual ID #. All our metal tags are made with a vintage Roover embosser.” The tradition starts with the founder himself — Orland White designed a tree-label making machine for the young arboretum, a gloriously complicated contraption that old hands describe as Rube Goldberg-like, and the habit it started — stamp it in metal, or don't bother — is still the rule today. Why metal? Because print fades, plastic shatters, and paint peels, but numbers pressed into aluminum can outlast the people who pressed them.

The same corner of trunk, as it actually hangs: #9558 standing vertical — and beside it, the torn fragment of an older tag being swallowed by the growing bark. Tap to enlarge.

❓ Why is the tag only on one side of the tree?

One tag is all a tree needs — the number is the name. Tags face the path side, so a curator walking the row can read every tree's name in one pass, without circling five hundred trunks. When you visit, look for them on the side you approach from.

❓ How high up are they — and does the height matter?

About chest height on a grown-up — call it roughly four feet up. It matters twice: high enough to read while standing (nobody should have to kneel in the leaf litter), and low enough to reach when a tag needs replacing. It is a working label, not a monument.

❓ What metal is it — and why not just print a label?

Aluminum: light, silvery, and it never rusts. And the letters are not printed on the tag, they are pressed into it by the embossing machine. Sun can bleach ink and frost can crack plastic, but a dent lasts. Some of the tags in this arboretum have been readable longer than most of us have been alive.

Two more tags, one after the other

On the same walk we stopped for these — read them against Blandy's own rule: one number for the group, one for the individual tree. These two read 10-10175 and 10-10176: same group, and individual numbers struck one right after the other — two trees catalogued in sequence as the crew worked its way along. Consecutive tags are how a collection thinks: not one famous tree at a time, but row after row, numbered like houses on a street.

Tag 10-10175, held flat to read. The numbers are not printed — they are pressed into the metal, so they stay legible for decades. Tap to enlarge.
And the next tree in the book: 10-10176. One digit on from its neighbor — the ledger, walking. Tap to enlarge.

❓ Does the nail hurt the tree?

About as much as a pinprick hurts you. The nail sits in the bark — the tree's dead outer coat, more like your fingernail than your skin. The living wood is deeper inside, and a healthy tree simply walls off a pin-sized wound and grows on. Here is the honest twist: the nail is not the tag's problem. Growth is.

❓ Then what happened to the broken tag in the photo?

The tree ate it — slowly. A trunk widens ring by ring, year after year. Bark creeps over nails, splits old plates, and curls them off the trunk like peeling paint. That torn fragment beside #9558 is an earlier tag mid-swallow. Replacing tags the trees have outgrown is part of the quiet maintenance rounds, forever — a collection of growing things can never be labelled once and for all.

❓ Why TWO numbers on every tag?

One number says when and with whom the plant arrived — its group and year, like a class year at school. The other is the tree's own ID — its personal name in number form. Arrival tells you the story of a planting; the ID tells you the story of a life. Our tag's line reads the ID: 9558.

❓ What if a tag falls off completely?

The tree is not lost. Every tree also lives on the arboretum's maps and in the records office, with its position fixed — so a missing tag can be re-struck with the right number and nailed back up. The number lives in the ledger first; the tag is just its copy on the trunk.

❓ Who actually reads these tags?

Curators checking health, researchers running experiments — the sex tally of this very grove was counted tag by tag — and you. Visitors can sponsor a grove ginkgo for $100 for five years, and the tree wears its sponsor's name, struck on the same vintage machine. Next time you pass a tag, stop and read it out loud. Somebody, decades ago, meant for you to.

Some tags carry the name outright: PINUS STROBIS — ID-1424, an Eastern White Pine. Species up top, personal number below: the whole system in one strip of metal. Tap to enlarge.
And some tags carry a thank-you: this grove ginkgo wears its sponsor's card — The Dood Squad, tree 2587, 2026 — tied on with a gold ribbon for the season. Sponsorship is the tag system turned outward: your name, on a tree, in the book. Tap to enlarge.

The Park and the People

The grove stands inside a much older story — an estate, a will, a scientist, and a promise the Commonwealth itself eventually signed. Four names explain the ground you walk on.

📍 712 acres🌳 172-acre arboretum🗓️ Willed to UVA in 1924🏛️ State Arboretum of Virginia, 1986🏷️ 5,000+ trees mapped & tagged

This land was the Tuleyries, the estate of Joseph Tuley Jr., who built the mansion in the 1830s. The 1840 census counted 73 enslaved people here — among the largest holdings in the area — and the east wing of the Quarters, built in the 1830s, served as the enslaved barracks. Ground-penetrating radar has since located an enslaved cemetery on the property with some 40 unmarked graves, and researchers are working to recover the names and stories of the people who lived and labored here. Any honest guide to this ground starts there.

The Tuleyries today: the 1830s mansion across the lawn, the Quarters standing beside it. The arboretum grew up in an estate's fields — the grove is a ten-minute walk from this grass. Tap to enlarge.
JT

Joseph Tuley Jr.

The builder · 1830s

He raised the Tuleyries mansion and assembled the estate whose fields, orchards, and quarters the arboretum still inhabits. The estate ran on enslaved labor — the Quarters outside the grove's shade are its surviving witness, and the recovery of the enslaved community's names is the farm's most important unfinished work.

Graham F. Blandy

The donor · died 1926

A New York stockbroker and railroad magnate who fell for this valley ground. His will gave 700 acres of the Tuleyries to the University of Virginia to train students in farming — and on his widow's death in 1939, a $670,000 endowment followed to keep the work alive. Everything in this guide grows on his gift.

Orland E. White

First director · 1927–1955

A plant geneticist fresh from hunting medicinal plants in the Amazon — that's him in the light suit, front left, in 1921. Hired in 1927, he built both the research station and the arboretum: 172 acres of labelled collections, the tag system this guide celebrates, and the ginkgo experiment itself. The arboretum carries his name because it is his work.

After lean decades, the arboretum opened fully to the public in the 1980s; in 1986 the Virginia General Assembly designated it the State Arboretum of Virginia, and the Foundation of the State Arboretum now partners in its care. Today it is curated under Director David Carr and Curator T'ai Roulston — among its charges North America's largest boxwood variety collection, a great conifer collection, the Cedar of Lebanon allée, and this grove.

Blandy's official arboretum map. Tap the map to open it big and scrollable — or take the PDF below. Map: Blandy Experimental Farm.

Visit: 400 Blandy Farm Lane, Boyce, Virginia 22620 — open every day, dawn to dusk, free. The Ginkgo Grove peaks in late October and early November; park near the Quarters and take the ten-minute walk through the Cedars of Lebanon.

Ginkgo and People

Two men bookend the ginkgo's modern story — one carried its name to the West, the other caught its oldest secret in the act. Between them runs a single thread: pay close attention to this tree, and it will teach you something nobody knew.

Engelbert Kaempfer

The messenger · 1690s

A German physician who reached Japan in the 1690s and wrote the ginkgo into Western science — the name, the description, the first seeds carried west. Tap his book's title page: at its foot sits a crest of three ginkgo leaves, three centuries before this grove was planted.

Sakugoro Hirase

The discoverer · 1896

A Japanese botanist who put ginkgo pollen under a microscope in 1896 and watched the tree's sperm swim — a living echo of the fern age, hidden inside a seed plant. Only ginkgoes and cycads still do this. The grove's fifty-year experiment in sex expression is, in a way, still answering his discovery.

🕊️

Survival as symbol. The Hiroshima ginkgo — blasted, burned, and budding again the next spring — made the species a living emblem of endurance; its seeds are planted worldwide as peace trees.

🧪

Survival as chemistry. The ginkgo's enormous genome carries armories of defensive compounds — the ginkgolides that discourage insects — the deep reason this species reads as nearly pest-free.

📊

Survival, tested. Leaf extract (EGb 761) is among the world's best-selling supplements, marketed for memory. When the claim met full-scale testing — the Ginkgo Evaluation of Memory study, over 3,000 older adults — it did not prevent dementia. The chemistry is real; the big promise failed the big test. Printing that plainly is itself a tribute to White's method.

🔬

Survival as science. Fossil ginkgo leaves are so common that scientists read their microscopic pores — stomata — as a barometer of ancient atmospheres, calibrating on living trees to reconstruct the air of the dinosaurs' world.

And one paradox to carry home: nearly every street ginkgo in the world is a clone — a grafted copy of a handful of male cultivars. A seed-grown grove like Blandy's, three hundred genetically distinct individuals, is therefore more than scenery. It is a reservoir of the species' variation — germplasm kept alive by records, tags, and patience.

Grow Your Own

Planting a ginkgo is a letter to the future — you are starting a tree that may live a thousand years. The good news: it asks very little. The one demand is the grove's whole lesson — drainage. Get that right and a ginkgo will forgive almost everything else.

☀️

Sun and room. Full sun, and space to become a 60–100 ft tree. Plant it like you mean forever — because you do.

🕳️

Dig wide, not deep. Two to three times the root ball's width, with the root flare exactly at ground level. If the hole holds water after rain, pick another spot — or another species: bald cypress.

💧

Water the first two summers. Deep drinks while the roots settle; after that, increasingly hands-off. Established ginkgoes shrug off drought that stresses lesser trees.

🏷️

Tag it. Write down what it is, where it came from, and when it went in. That single habit is the whole difference between a tree and a collection — you have seen what it built at Blandy.

SiteFull sun; room to become a 60–100 ft tree; away from pavement it can heave with age
HoleWide, not deep — two to three times the root ball's width; root flare exactly at grade
SoilNative soil backfill is fine; drainage is the deal-breaker — if the hole holds water, choose another spot (or another species: bald cypress)
WaterDeep watering through the first two summers; then increasingly hands-off
From seedClean the coat (gloves), cold-moist stratify 60–90 days, sow shallow; sex unknown for ~20 years
Guaranteed maleBuy a named grafted cultivar — 'Autumn Gold', 'Princeton Sentry', 'Saratoga'

From a seed you found — the grove way

🧤CLEANgloves on — the coat smells of rancid butter and can irritate skin
➜
❄️CHILL60–90 days cold and moist — winter, faked in the fridge
➜
🌱SOWshallow, in drained soil, in spring light
➜
⏳WAITsex stays secret ~20 years — that patience IS the Blandy experiment
🐾 A note for pet households: the fleshy seed coat and the nuts are not pet food — rake up fallen seeds where dogs roam, and keep the harvest for the kitchen, never the yard bowl.
